# NFAs to REX

This chapter's focus is on converting an NFA to a regular expression. By demonstrating the process of turning an NFA to a REX, you can see the underlying proof by construction that every NFA can be written has a REX. 

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning Objectives
- Understanding RIPs
- Understanding the relationsihp between NFAs and Regular Expressions
:::

## Converting an NFA into A Regular Expression

To convert an NFA into a regular expression, we will make use of yet another type of finite automata. In this automata, edges and transitions will occur on regular expressions rather than terminals. For example, if we could travel from A to B on "a,b", we will relabel this transition to "a+b" such that it matches the regular expression. In addition, we will be using an NFA that has a singular start state with no transitions to it and a singular accept state with no transitions leaving it. Let's create one of these as an example starting with a familiar DFA (see @Fig-RFAxM2) reproduced below.

::: {#fig-NFA2REXxM1}
::: {.light-content}
![](/images/RL/RFAxM2-black.svg)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](/images/RL/RFAxM2-white.svg)
:::

A simple deterministic finite automata (DFA).
:::

This DFA does not follow the rules of the specialized NFA that we require, so we'll make one. Add a new start state with an empty transition to the old start state and add a new accept state with an empty transition from the old accept state. This is still functionally the same machine, which is great news. Check out the new machine in @fig-NFAxRIP1.

::: {#fig-NFAxRIP1}
::: {.light-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP1-black.svg)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP1-white.svg)
:::

A new start and accept state have been added to the machine in @fig-NFA2REXxM1.
:::

At this point, our goal is to rip states out of this machine, repairing the transitions as needed so that we have a machine that recognizes the same language - just with one less state. In the end we should have only our new start and accept states. The transition between them will be the regular expression of the original machine. Let's start by ripping B out of the machine first. Let's take a look at B in @fig-NFAxRIP1b.

::: {#fig-NFAxRIP1b}
::: {.light-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP1b-black.svg)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP1b-white.svg)
:::

Ignoring some edges of @fig-NFAxRIP1 to highlight the node B.
:::

If we are going to remove B from this machine, we have to repair the transitions that a node may take through B. B has one transition in from A and two transitions out to A and E. This means, A can get back to itself by going through B. Also, A can get to E by going through B. In general, when removing a node, count the number of incoming transitions and outgoing transitions. The number of transitions that can happen through that node is the multiple of those two numbers. In this case, that is 1 and 2, and 1\*2=2. Let's look at the path from A to B to E. A to B is 1, B to itself is 1, and B to E is a free transition, ~. 
Using this, we can write a regular expression for the path from A to E. That regular expression is 11\*~ but since ~ is a free jump and concatenated with other termainls, we simply write this as 11\*. The first one is A to B, we star everything from B to itself (because we can take that 0 or more times) and then we concatenate on the transition from B to E. We'll do something similar with A to get 01\*0. Let's take a look at our new diagram, without B and using our regular expressions on the labels in @fig-NFAxRIP1c.

::: {#fig-NFAxRIP1c}
::: {.light-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP1c-black.svg)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP1c-white.svg)
:::

B has been removed from @fig-NFAxRIP1.
:::

Since A already had a path to itself, the new path that we found (through B) is added to the list of options for A to itself. On the contrary, since A did not have a transition to E before removing B, a new transition is added that encompasses, exhaustively, the path from A to E through B. Our next step is to remove A, which will leave us with only two states. The regular expression on that transition will be the regular expression of our original diagram. Let's try to rip A ourselves. The results are below.

<details>
<summary> The results of removing A from @fig-NFAxRIP1c.</summary>

::: {#fig-NFAxRIP1d}
::: {.light-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP1d-black.svg)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP1d-white.svg)
:::

The final regular expression of @fig-NFA2REXxM1.
:::

</details>

The original language of @fig-NFA2REXxM1 was any string with an odd number of 0's. Let's convince ourselves that this is true of the regular expression shown in @fig-NFAxRIP1d. The first loop allows a choice of any number of a 1 or two 0's with any number of 1's inside. This can be taken as many times as we like. Thus, to leave this expression, we know we will have seen an even number of 0's and any number of 1's. The last part of the expression is a single 0 followed by any number of 1s. So the first part forces an even number of 0's and the last bit adds a single 0 to make it odd. So, no matter what we have an odd number of 0s.

## A Second Example
Let's take a look at another example in @fig-NFAxM5. In this diagram, we see two accept states. The language is a bit complicated to describe, but our ripping process should give us a regular expression which can help with that. Before we begin our rips, see if you can see all the pathways that can lead to an accept state to describe this language.

::: {#fig-NFAxM5}
::: {.light-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxM5-black.svg)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxM5-white.svg)
:::

An interesting machine with a combination of a's, b's, c's and free jumps
:::


<details>
<summary> The starting point </summary>

To start we generally add a new start state and a new unique accept state. The new start state will have a free transition to the old start state and the original accept states will have free transitions to the new accept state.
Your resulting image should look like:

::: {.light-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP5-black.svg)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP5-white.svg)
:::

</details>

In general, removing nodes with less connections is easier. So we're going to rip in this order for this machine: A, C, E, B and then D. You can follow our steps below. If we remove states in a different order, we will very likely receive a different regular expression. Let's get started.

<details>
<summary> Removing A from above </summary>
We note that A has one incoming connection and two outgoing. So, we're looking at two expressions that either add a new connection or "or" into an existing connection.

::: {.light-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP5b-black.svg)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP5b-white.svg)
:::

</details>


<details>
<summary> Removing C from above </summary>
We see that C has one incoming and outgoing connection. Remember that concatentating with ~ simply does nothing, much like concatenating the empty string, "", results in the original string in most programming languages. This results in the following:

::: {.light-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP5c-black.svg)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP5c-white.svg)
:::

</details>

<details>
<summary> Removing E from above </summary>
Similarly E has one incoming and two outgoing connections. Let's remove it:

::: {.light-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP5d-black.svg)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP5d-white.svg)
:::

</details>

<details>
<summary> Removing B from above </summary>

Things start to get a little interesting because B has two incoming connections (from S and D) and two outgoing connections (to D and acc). This means 4 new pieces: S to D, D to D, S to acc, and D to acc. Most of these already have a connection so we'll be "or"ing in a new pathway.

::: {.light-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP5e-black.svg)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP5e-white.svg)
:::

</details>

<details>
<summary> Removing D from above </summary>

Our final step has only one in and one out, leaving us with a single connection from start to accept with our regular expression sitting on top. If you analyze this regular expression, the first part is the path to accept from A to B to C of our original machine. The longer part is more complicated. It's first part takes you from start to the state D. Then we have a loop for all the ways we can leave D and get back to D. Lastly we have the steps that can take us to an accept, either b (going to state E) or the final piece which takes us from D to E to B to C with each of it's looping bits in tact. Quite a complicated regular expression, but we can see how it encodes the language of the machine quite nicely. You can also see how the order of our RIPs leads to this breakdown of the loop that exists in the machine.

::: {.light-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP5f-black.svg)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](/images/RL/NFAxRIP5f-white.svg)
:::

</details>

It is time to get our hands dirty and try a few of our own.
